1247.title: More useful after death
1247.hook: dying, Dominic promised his brothers he'd help them more from heaven
1247.howItsDone: Catholics ask the saints to pray for them, in private prayer and in the Church's litanies; Dominicans traditionally sing the antiphon O Spem Miram to Saint Dominic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fra Angelico's cells: a quiet fresco in every friar's room. Your line was a painting in each cell.

Bologna, a friary, a hot summer. The founder is dying. Dominic, who by tradition walked the roads barefoot, and once talked all night with an innkeeper, lies on the floor, by tradition on sackcloth, too weak to rise. Around him his brothers are crying. They are young, the order is young, and they don't know how they'll manage without him. What do you say to people who are about to lose you? Dominic's answer was about the future, and it sounds almost cheeky.
screen: `BOLOGNA. THE FOUNDER IS DYING.` → `HIS BROTHERS ARE WEEPING.` → `LAST WORDS ABOUT THE FUTURE.`

segments.voice: An early life of Dominic, written by Jordan of Saxony, who led the order after him, tells it this way. Dominic saw his brothers weeping and told them not to. He would be more useful to them after his death, he said, than he had been in life. Not: I'll always be in your hearts. Not: carry on my work. But: I'm not leaving the job. I'm changing posts. Back on day ninety-six you met the cloud of witnesses; this is where it leads. The promise rests on a Catholic belief called the communion of saints. Catholics hold that the Church is one family across death: the living on earth, the dead being made ready, and the saints with God. And family members pray for one another. So asking a saint for help is, for Catholics, like asking a friend to pray for you, only the friend is now close to God. Hebrews, in the Douay-Rheims, pictures believers running their race "having so great a cloud of witnesses over our head." Christians don't all read this the same way. Catholic and Orthodox tradition asks the saints to pray. Some Protestant churches teach that prayer should go to God alone, and they honor the saints as examples rather than asking their help. Dominicans took Dominic at his word. Their tradition sings a short Latin antiphon to him that begins O spem miram, O wonderful hope, recalling this promise. A goodbye that turned into a job description.

If a loss is heavy right now, you don't have to carry it alone; in the US, 988 answers day and night, or reach local emergency help.

1248.title: Question everything
1248.hook: Dominican schools teach through structured argument
1248.howItsDone: Catholic seminaries and some university philosophy and theology courses still teach the Summa article by article, objections first, and some Dominican houses of study still argue questions out in structured debate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dominic's last promise to his weeping brothers: he'd be more useful after death. Your line was more useful then.

It seems that God does not exist. That is how Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican friar and a saint, opens his own question on whether God exists, in the book he wrote to teach beginners about God. Before he gives a single argument for God, he lays out objections against. If God is all good, why is there evil? And if nature can explain things on its own, why do we need God at all? He states them fairly, in plain words, as if a sharp student had raised a hand. Only then does he answer. That way of thinking has a name, and Dominican schools taught by it.
screen: `IT SEEMS THAT GOD DOES NOT EXIST.` → `THE OBJECTIONS COME FIRST.` → `THEN THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: You met Thomas, the quiet friar called the dumb ox, back on day eight hundred thirteen; today, his method. A disputation is a structured argument. In the universities where the friars taught, a master would set a question, students and other masters would raise objections, and then the master would weigh them and give an answer. The Summa of Thomas Aquinas is built like a disputation on paper. First, the question: whether such and such is so. Second, the objections, each beginning, it seems that. Third, on the contrary: a voice from scripture or tradition on the other side. Fourth, I answer that: Thomas's own reasoning. And last, the replies, where he goes back to every objection, one by one, often granting what's true in it. So you may not skip the hard question. You have to say the other side well enough that its friends would recognize it, and answer every objection, not just the weak ones. For Dominicans, this is not doubt for its own sake. It rests on a conviction that truth can stand being questioned, that faith and reason aren't enemies. Paul puts the instinct in one short line, in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Test first, then hold on.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you believe firmly, about faith, people, anything, and gently phrase the question a sharp friend might ask against it, beginning the way Thomas does: it seems that. Don't answer yet; just notice what's true in it, even a little. If you pray, bring the question to God as it is, unfinished.

1249.title: A Dominican day at home
1249.howItsDone: Lay Dominicans and others drawn to the order shape ordinary days around prayer, study and sharing, some praying morning and evening prayer from the Liturgy of the Hours and reading scripture or a spiritual book each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disputation: objections first, stated fairly, then the answer, then a reply to every one. Your line was a good question.

No friary. No white habit. No bell in a cloister calling anyone to choir. Just a kitchen, a phone on the counter, a commute, a shift, dinner, and dishes. For these last weeks this path has followed the Dominicans: an innkeeper up all night, nuns before friars, a motto of truth, a climber in Turin, a theologian who waited, a painter's quiet walls, a founder's last promise. Today is the last day with them, and it asks a small question. Could an ordinary day, in an ordinary house, have the Dominican shape?
screen: `NO FRIARY. JUST A KITCHEN.` → `WEEKS WITH THE DOMINICANS.` → `COULD A HOME DAY HAVE THEIR SHAPE?`

segments.voice: Here's the shape, in three motions. Morning: pray. It can be short. A Dominican at home might pray one psalm before the phone comes on. A psalm in the Douay-Rheims gives a line that fits: "O Lord, in the morning thou shalt hear my voice." Morning first, before the day gets its say. Midday: study. One page, chewed slowly: a Gospel passage, a paragraph of the catechism, a few lines of a saint. For the friars in the university towns, study wasn't a hobby beside prayer; it was prayer with the mind switched on. Evening: share one truth. Not a lecture. One true thing you learned or noticed today, handed to someone: at dinner, in a text, while folding laundry. That's the preacher in the house. Thomas Aquinas, the Dominican teacher, has a phrase for the whole pattern that Dominicans still quote: contemplata aliis tradere, to contemplate, and to hand on to others what you've contemplated. Prayer and study fill the cup. Sharing pours it out. If one of the three goes missing, the day tips: all prayer and no sharing turns inward, all sharing and no study runs dry. Tomorrow a new family arrives, the Jesuits, with a book of their own in hand.

1250.title: The Exercises
1250.hook: a month-long retreat in four weeks, guided by a director
1250.howItsDone: Catholics make the Spiritual Exercises at Jesuit and other retreat houses, either in a silent retreat of about a month with a director or in shorter adaptations; some make them in daily life over several months, meeting a director regularly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Dominican day at home, and the last day with Dominic's family. Your line was pray, study, share.

Here is a strange kind of book. Its author didn't write it for you to read. It's thin, full of numbered notes, lists and instructions for what to do next. Read straight through, it can feel like the rules of a sport you've never played. That's because it isn't a book to read. It's a book to use, by one person guiding another. The author was a Spanish soldier turned pilgrim named Ignatius of Loyola, and the friends who gathered around him became the Jesuits, the new family on this path. The book is where they start.
screen: `A BOOK NOT MEANT TO BE READ.` → `IGNATIUS OF LOYOLA.` → `THE JESUITS BEGIN HERE.`

segments.voice: Back on day two hundred thirty-seven, the examen came out of this same book. The Spiritual Exercises begin by explaining the name. Ignatius says: just as walking, marching and running are exercises for the body, so these are exercises for the soul, ways of preparing it to let go of disordered attachments, and then to seek and find what God wants for a life. Exercise, not information. You don't get fit reading about push-ups. The full retreat lasts about a month, kept in quiet, and it's divided into four parts Ignatius calls weeks. They aren't calendar weeks. They're stages, and a person may spend longer in one than another. In the first, the retreatant faces their own failures and God's mercy. In the second, they walk with Christ through his life. In the third, through his passion. In the fourth, they stay with the risen Christ. And no one makes this alone. The book is written for a director, a guide who meets the retreatant each day, offers the next exercise, listens, and adjusts. Ignatius even allows the Exercises to be made in daily life, a little each day over a longer time, for someone who can't leave home for a month. Jesus does something like it with his friends. After a busy mission, he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little." Apart, so you can hear.
screen: `WALKING AND RUNNING TRAIN THE BODY.` · `FOUR WEEKS: STAGES, NOT CALENDAR.` · `A DIRECTOR GUIDES EACH DAY.` · `OR IN DAILY LIFE, LITTLE BY LITTLE.` · then, large: `COME APART INTO A DESERT PLACE.`

segments.voice: Look at the weeks ahead and find one day, or half a day, or even two free hours, you could set apart. Picture where you'd go, a park bench, a church, a quiet room with the phone in a drawer, and who might be your guide afterward, a friend or a priest. If you pray, offer that day ahead of time.

1251.title: Principle and Foundation
1251.hook: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God
1251.howItsDone: Retreat directors give the Principle and Foundation to retreatants at the start of the Spiritual Exercises, and Jesuit schools and retreat programs return to it as a short statement of what a human life is for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Spiritual Exercises: a guided retreat in four stages called weeks, training the soul the way walking trains the body. Your line was exercises for the soul.

Why am I here? A child can ask it at bedtime. A teenager, slamming a door. A grown-up at three in the morning, or in a hospital corridor, or on the drive home from a job they don't love. It's an easy question to leave unanswered while the dishes wait. Ignatius doesn't leave it. Before the retreat's first week, before a single meditation on sin or mercy or the life of Christ, he sets one short paragraph at the door. It answers that question in a sentence, and everything after is built on top.
screen: `WHY AM I HERE?` → `ASKED AT BEDTIME AND AT 3 A.M.` → `ONE PARAGRAPH AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Ignatius calls it the Principle and Foundation, and it begins with the human person. In his words, put plainly: we are created to praise, to reverence, and to serve God our Lord, and by doing this to save our souls. Three verbs. Praise is the mouth: noticing and saying that something is good. Reverence is the posture: treating God, and the world God made, with care, not carelessness. Serve is the hands: doing something about it. Then the second move, and it's practical. Everything else on the face of the earth, Ignatius says, is created to help us toward that purpose. So things are tools, not goals. A career, a house, a reputation, even health: each is good to the degree it helps, and a problem to the degree it gets in the way. Tomorrow stays with what that asks. For today, notice the order: purpose first, then everything else measured against it. The book of Ecclesiastes, after a long search through pleasure and work and wisdom, comes to rest in a similar place, in the Douay-Rheims: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is all man." The whole of a person, in one line. A foundation is the part of a house nobody admires and everybody stands on. Get the bottom right, the paragraph suggests, and the rest of the building can go up.

1252.title: Indifference
1252.hook: not preferring health to sickness or long life to short, only what leads to God
1252.howItsDone: In Ignatian retreats, people pray for this inner freedom, which Ignatius calls indifference, before making a major decision, often with the help of a spiritual director.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Principle and Foundation: made to praise, reverence and serve God, with everything else a help or a hindrance. Your line was made for this.

I don't prefer health to sickness. Say that out loud and it sounds wrong. Yet a sentence like it sits near the very start of the Spiritual Exercises, right after yesterday's foundation. Ignatius of Loyola writes that a person should not want health more than sickness, riches more than poverty, honor more than dishonor, a long life more than a short one. Read fast, it sounds cold, even alarming. Read slowly, it's asking for something else. And his word for it does not mean what it means at a dinner party.
screen: `I DON'T PREFER HEALTH TO SICKNESS?` → `RIGHT AFTER THE FOUNDATION.` → `READ IT SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: In ordinary English, indifference is a shrug: whatever, I don't care. Ignatius means nearly the opposite. Go back to yesterday: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God, and the other things on earth are made to help us toward that end. Then comes the hinge. Use things as far as they help, and let them go as far as they hinder. To do that, he says, we have to make ourselves indifferent to all created things, wherever our free choice is allowed. Notice that last part. He isn't telling anyone to skip their medicine or turn down every raise. Where the choice isn't free, there is nothing to weigh. Where it is free, indifference keeps the scale level until you can see which way leads toward God. Then you choose, with your whole self. So this is not a lack of feeling. It's balance before a decision. A person can want health very badly and still hold that wanting open. Saint Paul says something close in his letter to the Philippians, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith." Learned. It took practice. Ignatius ends his sentence with the point: desiring and choosing only what leads more to the end for which we are made. Because the word can sound like numbness, some teachers reach for others: freedom, availability, open hands. Indifference doesn't make feelings vanish. It lets them speak, then asks one more question: which of these helps me love God and the people in front of me?
screen: `NOT A SHRUG.` · `USE THINGS AS FAR AS THEY HELP.` · `WHERE OUR FREE CHOICE IS ALLOWED.` · `BALANCE BEFORE A DECISION.` · then, large: `CONTENT IN WHATSOEVER STATE.`

chat.says: Doesn't Ignatius's indifference just mean not caring about anything?
options: No: it means holding free choices open, feelings and all, until you see which way leads to God.
Pretty much: it means you stop minding what happens, to you or to anyone else.
It means turning down good things, like a raise, just to prove you're detached from them.
chat.meaning: For Ignatius, indifference isn't a shrug; it's balance before a decision, where choice is free, desiring only what leads toward God.

1253.title: The first week
1253.hook: sin and mercy, ending in a conversation at the foot of the cross
1253.carry: what have I done for christ
1253.howItsDone: In the first week of an Ignatian retreat, people pray over sin and God's mercy, and end each prayer time with a colloquy, an unscripted conversation with Christ, often closed with the Our Father.

segments.voice: Yesterday, indifference: not a shrug, but balance, holding created things open until the way is clear. Your line was hold it loosely.

The first week of the Exercises is not gentle. Ignatius asks the person praying to look at sin, the world's and then their own, plainly, without excuses. Things said that can't be unsaid. It would be easy to get stuck there, in a pile of regret. He doesn't let it end there. At the close of the hour he moves the person to the foot of the cross, face to face, and talking. Not reciting. Talking. Today's word is the name he gives that talk.
screen: `LOOK AT SIN, PLAINLY.` → `DON'T STOP THERE.` → `GO TO THE FOOT OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: A colloquy is a conversation. Ignatius says to make it the way one friend speaks to another, or the way a servant speaks to a master: asking for something, admitting something, saying what's on your mind and asking advice. Imagine Christ our Lord in front of you, hanging on the cross. Ask how it is that the Creator became human, and went from eternal life to death, for my sins. Then turn to yourself with three questions. What have I done for Christ? What am I doing for Christ? What ought I to do for Christ? The week began with sin, and sin can turn a person inward, into shame. The colloquy turns them outward, toward a face. The questions are not a scorecard. They come after time spent looking at someone who loved first. Saint Paul has a line in Galatians that fits, in the Douay-Rheims: the Son of God, "who loved me, and delivered himself for me." Me, singular. Ignatius also asks the one praying to wonder that they've been allowed to go on living, that the earth has held them up, that mercy kept the door open. So the first week runs sin, then mercy, then conversation. Ignatius closes the colloquy with an Our Father, but the talk before it belongs to the one praying. Guilt alone tends to spin in place. A conversation goes somewhere.
screen: `COLLOQUY: A CONVERSATION.` · `AS ONE FRIEND SPEAKS TO ANOTHER.` · `THREE QUESTIONS AT THE CROSS.` · `SIN, THEN MERCY, THEN TALK.` · then, large: `WHO LOVED ME, AND DELIVERED HIMSELF FOR ME.`

segments.voice: If there's a crucifix nearby, look at it; if not, let the image come to mind. If you pray, speak to Christ in your own words, the way you'd talk to a friend at a hospital bedside, then let the first question sit: what have I done for Christ? If you don't pray, stay with the image of someone who gave something up for you, and ask what you've done in return.

Colloquy. A conversation, as one friend speaks to another, here at the foot of the cross. This week ran from Dominic's last promise to his brothers into the first week of Ignatius's Exercises. Today's word.
Your line: what have I done for Christ. The other two questions follow: what am I doing, and what ought I to do. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1253 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CALL OF THE KING.`

chat.says: What do you actually say to Christ at the end of that first-week prayer?
options: Whatever's true, as one friend speaks to another, then ask: what have I done for Christ?
A set prayer Ignatius wrote out, recited exactly, so that you don't say the wrong thing.
You explain why each sin wasn't really your fault, so Christ can see your side.
chat.meaning: The colloquy is a real conversation, like one friend to another; Ignatius doesn't script it, and closes it only with an Our Father.
